decisions.routing: Sibling skills covering the same trigger must each state the discriminator and name the alternative. executing-plans and subagent-driven-development both key on subagent availability; using-git-worktrees and dispatching-parallel-agents explicitly disclaim plan execution.
decisions.uses-graph: Every skill named in another skill's description, body, or companions is declared in that skill's uses: block. Bare sibling names in prose are backticked so a name is visually distinct from an ordinary word.
decisions.uses-is-agent-facing: Verified against skills@1.5.23 dist/cli.mjs: the installer parses only name and description; 'uses' appears nowhere. uses: survives installs because unknown keys are ignored, not because anything acts on it. decisions.standalone: Verified by enumeration, not sampling: all 24 declared dependency edges were exercised with the target skill absent, across four isolated installs. decisions.diagrams: Diagrams are mermaid fences, not graphviz. graphviz needs a `dot` binary that is not installed here, so the 11 dot fences were unrendered source text; mermaid renders natively in GitHub, VS Code, and agent UIs. decisions.mermaid-validation: Validated against mermaid 11.17.2: Pass A mermaid.parse under jsdom 9/9; Pass B mermaid.render in real Chromium 9/9 with no error-SVG and min SVG 13,895 bytes (real diagrams, not stubs). Both passes teeth-checked 5/5 against unclosed brackets, misspelled type, ':: ' in state label, ';' in sequence message, malformed ER cardinality. Silent-pitfall scan clean; parenthesised labels confirmed verbatim via getDiagramFromText. Note: this repo pins no mermaid dependency and has no CI check, so GitHub's renderer version may differ.

decisions.source-rejections: Leonxlnx/taste-skill REJECTED: self-scopes to marketing pages ('NOT for: Dashboards / dense product UI / admin panels'), prescribes a visual style that following-repo-ui-conventions:19 forbids inventing, 1207-line body against a <1000-word target. designmotionhq.com/patterns REJECTED as a source: quality spread within one site - z-index-mastery is correct CSS mechanics while golden-ratio is myth ('seashells, galaxies', unsourced Stripe/Linear claim) whose 1.618 type scale contradicts the measured typography rules; unsourced motion ms dials conflict with exact values held elsewhere. One verified line adopted: stacking-context behaviour into building-responsive-layouts. jakub.kr blog articles superseded by his skills repo, which is the same author's material in reviewable form. REVISITED 2026-09-08: designmotionhq.com/patterns re-crawled in full (76 detail pages via browser, not the index) and audited against the corpus. The original rejection holds for the source as a whole and for its numeric motion dials specifically - a primary-source check found no published basis for any duration figure, Apple publishes none at all, and Material moved from prose bands to per-component numbers to a token scale published without the prose thresholds earlier versions carried. The commonly repeated derivation from the 100ms response-time limit is a scope error: that figure bounds when a system starts responding, not how long motion runs. Nine mechanism-level gaps were adopted on their own merit rather than on the site's authority, plus two rules from pages previously rejected wholesale. Two motion rules are sourced: the enter-decelerates/exit-accelerates split and shorter exits, both stated by Material across three versions with a rationale, and the reduced-motion obligation for scroll-linked motion, which comes from WCAG SC 2.3.3 (AAA) rather than the scroll-animations spec, whose normative text imposes none. cursor/plugins audited in full on 2026-09-09: 90 first-party skills across 15 plugins, plus 66 third-party SaaS integrations ignored as out of scope. Most first-party skills are product-coupled (Cursor canvases, SDK, cloud agents, voice) or gh-command recipes. pstack's 23 principle-* skills are the closest match to this corpus and are mostly duplicates of existing owners - root-cause debugging, prove-it-works, subtract-before-you-add, test-behaviour-not-implementation. Three items adopted: cli-for-agents as a new skill (MIT, attributed, rewritten), the INCONCLUSIVE verification outcome into verifying-before-completion, and the anchoring guard into requesting-code-review. The audit's most valuable finding was about this corpus rather than theirs: systematic-debugging/references/defense-in-depth.md said validate at EVERY layer while cleaning-ai-slop said validate at boundaries only and listed internal validation as slop to delete. Both now state their scope - layered validation is earned by a demonstrated bug, speculative internal checks are not.

decisions.description-conventions: Audited 2026-09-06 against the rules the corpus actually codifies in writing-skills (third person, trigger phrase, name matches directory) rather than invented ones. Note: an earlier pass flagged em dashes and curly quotes across 40 files; that standard is NOT codified anywhere in this repo and those files were left alone. Style rules that no document states are not violations. Follow-up: writing-skills' checklist said descriptions must start with 'Use when...' while its own prose and the README said only 'states when to use'. Two skills legitimately open with 'Use before' (brainstorming, using-git-worktrees) because they run ahead of their trigger rather than in response to it, so the checklist and README were aligned to that reality instead of forcing 25-of-27 phrasing onto two accurate descriptions. Rejected in the same pass: a claim that the corpus bans hyphens in descriptions in favour of em dashes. No such rule exists anywhere; the only hyphen rules in writing-skills govern the name field.
decisions.jakub-kr-site-sweep: Browser-driven sweep of jakub.kr on 2026-09-07, after the user asked whether earlier passes had missed anything. They had. Prior surveys read 11 pages found by BFS link-crawling; the sitemap lists 16 and the union is 15 real pages (~13,900 words, 79 headings). Five substantial rule-bearing pages had never been read at all: /components/oklch-colors, /work/gradients, /work/drag-gesture, /work/motion-gestures, /work/shared-layout-animations. Worse, /writing/details-that-make-interfaces-feel-better had been mined for ONE section (shadows-instead-of-borders, now designing-component-systems:85) while its ten sibling sections were skipped - the crawl was section-blind, extracting only where a rule matched something already being looked for. decisions.rust-corpus: Added 2026-09-07: five Rust skills as original text restating mechanisms from MIT-licensed sources, not forked. Skills: writing-idiomatic-rust (ownership, clones, fallibility, error-type design, iterators, dispatch), reviewing-unsafe-rust (what each unsafe operation requires, soundness preconditions, FFI), writing-async-rust (cancellation, state across await points, blocking, task lifetime), hardening-rust-supply-chain (dependency policy, lockfiles, advisories), speeding-up-rust-builds (critical path, crate graph, dev profiles). Licensing: actionbook/rust-skills (1.4k stars, the obvious candidate) has NO LICENSE file and the GitHub API reports license:null despite a README MIT badge, so its text carries no grant; its adoptable content is also coupled to a router/hook plugin system. Sources used had their MIT text read in-tree: apollographql/skills, mohitmishra786/low-level-dev-skills, Rust-Coding-Guidelines/rust-coding-guidelines-zh. writing-async-rust has no upstream: no surveyed source covered cancellation semantics. Rejected by scope: actionbook m01-m15 meta-cognition (routing scaffolds, not checkable rules), actionbook domain-* and tool wrappers (crate recipes and vendor CLI wrappers), actionbook's Deprecated table ('std::sync::Mutex -> parking_lot' with no reason or version), apollo's Quick Reference (bare assertions; reasons live only in the chapters), apollo-router-plugin-creator (product surface), trailofbits rust-review (orchestration harness stating no rules), rust-no-std (substantive but no consumer here). Verification: claims that compile were compiled. 10 cases under rustc stable including two negatives that must fail (Vec<T> to &[T]; non-Send held across an await). That sweep found one defect - the ownership section claimed a &str parameter accepts a String, which is E0308; deref coercion covers &String. Structural gates (frontmatter, graph parity, hashes, mermaid) cannot see a false claim, so tool and language facts are verified against primary sources instead.
decisions.rust-tool-facts: Verified 2026-09-07 against primary sources (cargo-deny 0.20.2 and cargo-audit 0.22.2 books plus their source; the Cargo Book, rustc book, and Rust blog). Corrected five defects the structural gates could not see. (1) Neither cargo-deny nor cargo-audit supports an ignore expiry: IgnoreId takes only id + reason and finalizes with deny-unknown-fields, so `expires` is a parse error, and cargo-audit's ignore is a bare Vec<Id>; the skill had recommended recording an expiry. (2) 'Set each policy to deny' was incoherent - vulnerabilities, unlicensed, and non-allowed licences are hardcoded Severity::Error with no key, and unmaintained takes a Scope enum, not a lint level. (3) wildcards defaults to allow, not warn; the book's prose is a doc bug contradicted by source and by the maintainers' deny.template.toml. (4) The bin/lib lockfile split was officially retired 2023-08-29 and cargo new no longer ignores lockfiles for libraries. (5) rust-lld has been the default on x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu since 1.90, so -fuse-ld=lld is stale there; also debug=1 is 'limited' not line-tables-only, lto=false is not 'off', codegen-backend is nightly-only, and opt-level>=2 on dependencies stops monomorphised generics being shared across crates. Also corrected: the crate-graph section had led with 'break circular dependencies first', but cargo rejects package cycles at resolution (measured: `error: cyclic package dependency`, exit 101), so that build cannot exist. Replaced with the real constraint - a split must follow a one-way dependency, and the only legal cycle is through dev-dependencies, which costs build ordering under cargo test. Version anchors added to the skills themselves, not just this record: the cargo-deny lint table is marked 'Verified against cargo-deny 0.20.2' and carries a note that the schema moves (unmaintained became a scope; vulnerability, severity-threshold and unlicensed were removed), the expiry finding names cargo-deny 0.20.2 / cargo-audit 0.22.2, and the debug ladder names the 1.71 MSRV for the string forms. Without an anchor a reader cannot tell a schema change from an error in the skill, and because these configs reject unknown keys a stale key fails the build rather than being ignored.
decisions.rust-async-runtime-scope: Verified 2026-09-07 against std docs, tokio 1.53.1, async-std 1.13.2, smol 2.0.2 / async-task 4.7.1, plus direct measurement. writing-async-rust originally stated tokio behaviour as universal. Findings: (1) DIVERGENCE - dropping a task handle detaches under tokio and async-std but CANCELS under smol and anything on async-task, which marks Task #[must_use = "tasks get canceled when dropped"]. Measured: identical spawn-drop-wait shape runs under tokio and never runs under smol. The skill had asserted the tokio behaviour as universal, which is inverted for half the ecosystem. (2) 'Cancellation safety' is tokio's own term, defined on its select! docs; std and futures-rs do not use it, and the per-API verdicts are tokio's about tokio's APIs. (3) Tokio's own Mutex docs say 'Contrary to popular belief, it is ok and often preferred to use the ordinary Mutex from the standard library in asynchronous code', contradicting the skill's blanket 'needs an async-aware lock'. (4) A non-Send value across an await is compiler-level, not runtime-level, and under spawn_local it compiles and runs correctly - measured; the skill had wrongly attached a deadlock to it. The real deadlock is a blocking guard held across an await on a single-threaded runtime, measured as a total hang in which a 400ms tokio::time::timeout never fired because the timer could not run. (5) block_in_place is multi-threaded-only and panics on a current-thread runtime; std provides no offload facility at all. Language-level claims (lazy polling, cancel-by-drop, auto-trait derivation) are now separated from runtime-specific ones, and versions are anchored in the overview. Lock guidance sharpened after review: the two directions have different force and were measured separately. std Mutex by default is a preference (tokio's own docs). An async lock when the guard spans an await is a REQUIREMENT: a std guard is not Send, so under tokio::spawn it is a hard compile error ('future cannot be sent between threads safely', measured exit 101), while the identical code under spawn_local compiles and runs (measured exit 0) and fails instead as the runtime hang. Same rule, different enforcement; the skill now states both directions in the body, checklist and anti-patterns.
decisions.rust-unsafe-verification: Verified 2026-09-07 against stable Rust 1.90 by compiling every checkable claim; reviewing-unsafe-rust had shipped with no verification pass. Confirmed: all five classic capabilities are genuinely gated (E0133 for deref/unsafe-call/mutable-static/union-field, E0200 for unsafe trait impl, each proven by a without-unsafe negative that fails and a with-unsafe positive that compiles); safe rules stay in force inside an unsafe block (a use-after-borrow is still E0502); Send/Sync are auto-derived, a manual impl without unsafe is E0200, and a raw-pointer struct is not auto-Send (E0277). Corrected: (1) 'exactly five capabilities' is wrong - inline assembly is also gated by E0133, and in edition 2024 attributes such as #[no_mangle] require an unsafe(...) wrapper, so five is the historical framing not the current count; the overview asserted this too. (2) 'A Rust panic unwinding into foreign frames is undefined behaviour' is outdated - since Rust 1.81 it aborts (measured: exit 134 SIGABRT). The advice to catch at the boundary stands; the stated mechanism did not. Strengthened with measurement: repr(Rust) genuinely reorders a u8,u32,u8 struct to offsets 4/0/5 against repr(C)'s 0/4/8 and is smaller (8 vs 12 bytes); a crate with an out-of-bounds read and a double-&mut passes cargo test 2/2 green while cargo miri test reports 'error: Undefined Behavior' and exits 1, and clippy on the same UB exits 0 with zero warnings - the skill's claim that a clean lint run is no evidence about unsafe correctness is now demonstrated rather than asserted. Also noted that miri halts at the first violation, so a clean rerun does not prove there was only one.
decisions.rust-build-measured-from-practice: Updated 2026-09-07 from a real workspace's .cargo/config.toml and Cargo.toml (TheGrid, 24 crates, nightly-2026-08-18) whose settings carry their own measurements. Two corrections and two additions. CORRECTION 1: the skill said rust-lld is the default since 1.90 and treated that as toolchain-wide; it is per-target. Verified with `rustc --print link-args` on this box: the host aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu target links via plain `cc` with no fuse-ld flag, and `fuse-ld=lld` appears only when -Clinker-features=+lld is passed explicitly. The 1.90 change landed for x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu only. CORRECTION 2: two paragraphs contradicted each other after the first edit - one saying lld is already on, the next saying 'if you do switch to lld'. Resolved into a single per-target rule. ADDITION 1: the lld thread-oversubscription trap, which the skill omitted entirely and which inverts the advice. lld defaults to one thread per core PER LINK while cargo links concurrently; measured on a 12-core box relinking 33 test binaries, GNU bfd 38.3s, lld --threads=1 13.1s, lld default threads 120-150s - the fast linker was 4x SLOWER than the one it replaced until capped. ADDITION 2: debug-info numbers with a verified backtrace-parity claim - debug=true 29.2s, line-tables-only 10.1s, debug=0 6.6s, with 41 resolved frames under both true and line-tables-only and 0 under debug=0, so the 2.9x costs debugger variable inspection rather than backtraces; plus the per-session CARGO_PROFILE_DEV_DEBUG=true override and the [profile.bench] exemption that profilers need. Follow-up 2026-09-07 after a reviewer questioned whether the rust-lld default claim and its anti-pattern were true at all. Verified against the 1.90.0 release notes, PR #140525, the rustc book, and compiler source; plus measured locally. Three further corrections. (a) The default is narrower than 'x86_64 since 1.90': it is applied via a bootstrap env var (CFG_DEFAULT_LINKER_SELF_CONTAINED_LLD_CC) only for x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu and only in the toolchains rustup distributes, so a distro-built rustc may not have it. (b) -Clinker-features=+lld is unstable on EVERY target including x86_64 and errors without -Zunstable-options - measured here as 'error: `-C linker-features=+lld` is unstable'; only the -lld opt-out is stable, and only on x86_64. The skill had presented +lld as an ordinary knob. (c) The anti-pattern 'Adding -fuse-ld=lld where rust-lld is already the default' was WRONG: the rustc book states 'If the user also passes a -Clink-arg=-fuse-ld=$value, both will be given to the linker driver but the user's will be passed last, and would generally have priority over rustc's', so it is redundant and harmless rather than conflicting. Replaced with the real hazard - using a -fuse-ld override as an opt-out instead of the supported -Clinker-features=-lld, noting that rustc's old-GCC retry strips only the exact string -fuse-ld=lld so a differently-spelled override survives a retry meant to drop it.
decisions.corpus-review-2026-09-07: Full 33-skill review for rendering and structural defects. Checked: fence closure and tagging, fence languages, table/heading/list blank-line separation, bare URLs, backtick balance, paragraph length and prose runs, heading depth, emoji, all-caps, trailing whitespace, TODO markers, and heading vocabulary. Fixed three real defects: (1) systematic-debugging's h2 read '## your human partner's Signals You're Doing It Wrong', ungrammatical damage from an earlier find-and-replace de-personalisation pass; (2) one trailing-whitespace line in writing-skills; (3) twelve headings across eight skills that differed only in casing - 'When To Use'/'When to Use' vs 'When to use', 'Anti-Patterns' vs 'Anti-patterns', 'Red flags' vs 'Red Flags', 'Common mistakes' vs 'Common Mistakes' - normalised to the corpus-majority form, with no internal anchor links or prose references to break. Deliberately NOT changed: the `dot` fence at writing-skills:281, which the `diagrams` decision records as the one deliberately-bad example kept as graphviz because the section heading is '### Code in Flowcharts' and the fence IS the anti-pattern; 30 untagged fences, which hold pseudo-code process templates and directory trees rather than runnable code; and the semantic split between 'Anti-patterns' (12), 'Red Flags' (5) and 'Common Mistakes' (5), which mark genuinely different things in workflow skills. No unclosed fences, no oversized paragraphs (longest 107 words), no h4+ nesting outside two skills, and no broken tables were found. SECOND PASS: the first review only opened SKILL.md files and its fence scan matched `{3,}, so it was structurally blind to malformed delimiters. A reviewer caught 68 two-backtick fence lines across 5 files in testing-skills (SKILL.md, examples/claude-md-test-campaign.md, references/bulletproofing.md, references/persuasion-principles.md, references/testing-with-subagents.md), including tagged opens like ``markdown and ``yaml, all of which render as inline code rather than blocks - 34 blocks broken. Verified before converting: every file balanced (opens == closes), zero pre-existing three-tick fences, zero mid-line double-backtick spans that a ^`` pass could clobber, and no nested fences needing longer delimiters. Converted all 68 and confirmed content byte-identical apart from the added tick. Also swept all 73 markdown files (33 SKILL.md + 40 companions) for single-backtick line starts, unclosed fences, trailing whitespace, consecutive blanks, lowercase headings and missing trailing newlines; the remaining flags were all false positives - prose lines wrapping onto a backticked term, and legitimate headings ('# iOS input zoom recipes', '# advanced.md'). Root-caused the miss: the corpus-wide grep used the BRE `^``\([^`]\|$\)`, which returns 0 rather than erroring. Verified against the pre-fix file at 70e1fd2 - that pattern finds 0 matches while `grep -P '^``(?!`)'` and `grep '^``' | grep -v '```'` both find 12. Isolated the failing construct: `^``[^`]` alone matches and `^``` alone matches, but the escaped alternation inside the group yields 0 under BOTH BRE and ERE, and `\|` is alternation in BRE yet a literal pipe in ERE, so the pattern was never portable. The silent zero sent the investigation to symlinks and git-tracking before the JS scan settled it. Rule going forward: a zero result from a hand-written regex is a claim that needs a positive control - run the pattern against content known to contain the target before believing an empty result. THIRD PASS, closing the two items the review measured but left: (1) ten sentence-initial 'your human partner' artifacts across five files - the same find-and-replace damage as the systematic-debugging heading - capitalised, with the 13 legitimate mid-sentence uses preserved. (2) The Rust skills were the corpus's prose-heaviest at 79% prose against a 34% average, four of five with zero tables while the UI skills carry '## Detection patterns' tables throughout. Final state across the five skills - 58 table rows, 31 anti-patterns, 41 checklist items, maximum cross-section overlap 0.33, verified over all three pairings including anti-pattern against checklist. The corrected detector renders each candidate block and carries a positive control proving it can fire. upstreamRetrieval: Upstream bytes are fetched on demand at the pinned SHA rather than vendored into this repo: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/<repo>/<sha>/<path>. Every upstream file records its sha256 here, so a drift check verifies the fetched bytes without trusting the network. A vendor-snapshot/ directory previously held these bytes; it was removed as bloat (1.2MB, 134 files) after verifying the fetched blobs are byte-identical to the snapshot and that vendor-snapshot/local duplicated content already in git history at f7b6fdf.

lockfileNotes.computedHashAlgorithm: sha256 over the whole skill DIRECTORY, not SKILL.md. From skills@1.5.25 dist/cli.mjs computeSkillFolderHash: collect every file recursively (skipping .git and node_modules), sort by relative path with localeCompare, then for each file update the hash with the relative path string followed by the file bytes.
lockfileNotes.whyItMatters: Hashing SKILL.md alone makes every multi-file skill look stale, and single-file skills too, since the path string is fed in as well. That false signal reads exactly like real drift across the whole lock and invites a mass rewrite that would overwrite correct pins.
lockfileNotes.installerBehaviour: experimental_install PRESERVES an existing computedHash and only computes one when the key is absent. A stale pin therefore never self-corrects through reinstalling; it must be recomputed deliberately.
lockfileNotes.verifiedOn: 2026-09-10 against Tickify skills-lock.json: 65/66 reproduced exactly, isolating one genuinely stale pin (find-skills).
lockfileNotes.corpusIsUniform: Every audacioustux/agents skill is installed in every consumer repo, without curating by host language or stack. Skills are read on demand and each self-scopes in its description, so an irrelevant one costs a lock row and some disk but nothing at runtime. A divergent corpus costs correctness: when the two consumer locks disagreed about which corpus names existed, the result was nine stale names that silently failed to install and masked further rot behind the installer's first-dead-path abort. Per-repo curation applies to third-party entries only — Tickify carries es-toolkit's guide and recommend because it depends on es-toolkit; TheGrid does not. Audited 2026-09-10: Tickify has zero .rs files and all 5 Rust skills; that is deliberate, not drift.
lockfileNotes.nextjsGapAudited: 2026-09-10: Tickify runs Next 16.3.4 / React 19 and no installed skill covers either. Searched the registry; every Next.js skill offered is community-authored, none from Vercel, which is a different trust class from prisma/prisma or firecrawl/cli teaching their own products. Read the most-installed candidate (wshobson/agents@nextjs-app-router-patterns, 29.5K installs): it targets "Next.js 14+", is 3.6KB, and covers none of async params, use cache, or PPR. Tickify's own code already uses params: Promise<> with await params — the Next 15+ shape the skill predates — so installing it would teach patterns this codebase has moved past. Rejected. The gap is real and stays open; a Vercel-authored skill, or a corpus-owned one written against 16, would close it.
lockfileNotes.linkAudit: 2026-09-10: audited every relative markdown link across all installed skills in both consumers, prompted by finding dead monorepo links in prisma-8. Corpus result: zero dead links outside fenced blocks. Two classes of false positive a naive checker reports and must not 'fix': paths inside fenced blocks illustrating a hypothetical skill's own layout (FORMS.md, reference/finance.md in writing-skills — correct as written), and site-absolute paths copied from a vendor's docs, which are real defects since they resolve against the filesystem root when read from a skills directory. Remaining dead links live only in non-corpus skills: prisma-8 (12, upstream monorepo pointers, kept because none gates a procedure) and pci-secure-software (29, unmanaged local skill).
